steps.label: Enterprise walkthrough: distinguish plan, subscription, cycle and occurrence
steps.detail: A plan describes an offer; a customer subscription records participation; a billing cycle groups financial eligibility; an occurrence represents a particular scheduled meal obligation. They must not be represented as one mutable status. Read the Subscription README and PlanScheduleService. getPublicActive checks that the plan exists and is ACTIVE, then retrieves its active schedule and constructs a public response. Its item mapping includes menu identity/name/category/food type, price/currency, quantity, recurrence positions, meal slot, service time and sequence. Follow the response DTO rather than assuming every internal schedule field is public. A publicly visible plan does not prove that a particular customer is subscribed or has paid for an occurrence.

steps.label: Enterprise failure analysis: avoid deriving financial eligibility from visibility
steps.detail: Create a synthetic active plan with no customer subscription, a subscription with no paid cycle, and a paid cycle whose occurrence is not yet eligible for fulfillment. Explain the missing record or policy at each stage. Do not turn public plan visibility into order creation. A chef's relationship to a plan and a customer's ownership of a subscription are distinct access boundaries. Record which identifiers the caller controls and which are derived from the verified principal. Source defaults, feature flags and lifecycle policy must be checked separately from the presence of a Java class.

steps.label: Enterprise lab: reconstruct a subscription's record chain
steps.detail: Draw a synthetic plan-to-subscription-to-cycle-to-occurrence-to-order sequence with unique IDs and separate states. Read SubscriptionServiceOwnershipTest and ChefPlanEndpointOwnershipTest. Run mvn -B -ntp -f services/subscription-service/pom.xml -Dtest=SubscriptionServiceOwnershipTest,ChefPlanEndpointOwnershipTest test. Document exactly which owner/role cases these tests exercise. Add a local wrong-owner fixture using the existing test style and verify that it fails before an unrelated customer's subscription is exposed. Do not create a real plan, enroll a customer, charge a cycle or enable an occurrence worker.

lessons.lab: Completion evidence: the complete record chain, owner boundaries and test results. Explain why an ACTIVE plan is not proof of payment or permission to fulfill every scheduled meal.

steps.label: Enterprise walkthrough: mark the boundary between mechanism and policy
steps.detail: Scheduling code can represent recurrence and lifecycle transitions, but product owners decide pricing, entitlement, pauses, skips, cancellation, refunds and meal credits. Create a policy ledger linking each needed decision to its approved architecture/functional-spec section. A default in an old example is not a product approval. The inspected PlanScheduleService's internal get operation permits PLATFORM_ADMIN or SUBSCRIPTION_ADMIN and checks plan existence. That access mechanism does not define the commercial consequences of changing a schedule. Trace the actual write service before explaining any lifecycle action, and keep proposed training scenarios clearly labeled as proposals rather than describing them as deployed Craves behavior.

steps.label: Enterprise failure analysis: missing policy must not become a guessed rule
steps.detail: For a request to pause meals, ask which cycle and occurrences it affects, whether fulfillment was already created, what happens to captured money and who can perform the action. Do not answer those business questions by extrapolating from a status name. When code deliberately disables a capability without approved policy, preserve that fail-closed behavior. Do not seed schedule, refund or entitlement policy rows during an unrelated release. An administrator's ability to read a schedule is not authorization to modify a customer's financial position. Changes must retain the existing audit, ownership and idempotency contracts.

steps.label: Enterprise lab: produce a policy-to-test matrix
steps.detail: Use a fictional request for a schedule display improvement, then contrast it with a pause/refund request. Classify each acceptance criterion as presentation, access control, persistence, timing or product-owned financial policy. For unknown business decisions, write an explicit unresolved entry instead of a default value. Read the Subscription policy visibility and ownership tests and identify the implemented boundaries. Provide test scenarios that can be written now, and scenarios blocked on an approved rule. The exercise should teach how to move engineering forward without manufacturing policy; it must not update live plans or policy tables.

lessons.lab: Completion evidence: a policy ledger with known, proposed and unresolved decisions separated. The reviewer should reject a solution that hides a guessed refund or meal-credit rule inside a scheduler or UI.

steps.label: Enterprise walkthrough: follow recurrence through time and ownership
steps.detail: Read PlanScheduleService's public and administrative reads with the schedule models and repository. Identify recurrence type, timezone, ISO day of week, day of month, meal-slot code, service time and sequence number as separate fields. A local wall-clock meal time is not identical to a UTC instant. Follow the occurrence-generation and paid-cycle safety tests to see how the source implementation handles eligibility and replay. Do not assume monthly day 31, daylight-saving transitions or a missed worker run have the behavior you prefer; inspect the implementation and approved policy. A scheduler waking up is not proof that every eligible occurrence was safely committed.

steps.label: Enterprise failure analysis: restarts and time boundaries
steps.detail: Construct timelines for a worker restart, a repeated run, a delayed payment signal and a date boundary in the schedule's timezone. Identify a stable occurrence identity and the stored state that prevents duplicated fulfillment. A process-local timer cannot preserve exactly what work completed before a crash. Read the relevant repository constraints and claim/transaction behavior before claiming concurrency safety. Keep financial eligibility checked at the correct point; an occurrence should not become fulfillable just because a cycle record exists. Document the distinction between source support for a timezone and a tested set of timezone/date edge cases.

steps.label: Enterprise lab: design deterministic time-based tests
steps.detail: Run mvn -B -ntp -f services/subscription-service/pom.xml -Dtest=PlanScheduleRequestValidationTest,OccurrencePaidCycleSafetyTest test after inspecting their fixtures. Build a synthetic table for ordinary day, month boundary, repeated execution, missing paid cycle and a late-arriving eligibility signal. Use fixed clocks or explicit timestamps in new local tests rather than sleeps. For every row, record expected occurrence count, order-call count and state. Do not use the real current date as an undocumented dependency. The evidence must distinguish a pure unit decision from a database constraint or worker integration test not yet executed.

lessons.lab: Completion evidence: deterministic time/eligibility scenarios and a request-to-occurrence sequence. A correct explanation accounts for restart and replay without inventing the commercial treatment of missed meals.

steps.label: Enterprise walkthrough: implement a read-only schedule preview
steps.detail: Training-only feature brief: present the existing public active-plan schedule in a clearer preview without generating occurrences or changing entitlement. Begin with PlanScheduleService.getPublicActive and PublicPlanScheduleResponse. Identify the exact existing API endpoint and client consumer through the controller; do not invent a URL based on the service method. Define presentation for weekly versus monthly recurrence, sequence order, missing optional information and an inactive/unavailable plan. Keep the backend's ownership of schedule facts and current public projection. The client may format a value for display but must not decide payment eligibility or silently convert an unknown recurrence into an active meal.

steps.label: Enterprise failure analysis: public projections and unknown data
steps.detail: The public view must not expose private subscription or administrator fields. Test inactive plan, missing active schedule, empty schedule items where permitted by the real contract, unknown future recurrence and malformed response. Distinguish a plan that is not available from an infrastructure failure. A preview must not call the occurrence generator or create orders on page load. Sorting for presentation must preserve the authoritative sequence semantics. If an additional backend field is proposed, explicitly define backward compatibility and avoid a schema change when an existing public field already carries the needed information.

steps.label: Enterprise lab: build and test the preview locally
steps.detail: Create training/subscription-schedule-preview. Write response-parser and presentation tests using synthetic PublicPlanScheduleResponse values. Implement loading, ready, unavailable and retryable-error states in the selected web or mobile client. Add a spy/mock assertion proving that no occurrence/order/payment mutation occurs during a read. Run the relevant client tests and typecheck plus the focused schedule/ownership Java tests. Submit full changed files, synthetic screenshots or response examples, access/privacy assertions and a rollback note. Do not modify schedule policy, public activation state, billing, existing customer subscriptions or runtime worker flags.

lessons.lab: Completion evidence: a working local preview, negative response tests and an explicit no-side-effect assertion. The learner must explain why display work does not justify modifying billing or occurrence-generation policy.

steps.label: Enterprise walkthrough: release schema and workers independently
steps.detail: A subscription release can contain schema, public APIs, billing consumers, occurrence generation and order callbacks. Deploying code does not require activating every dormant worker. Verify the target migration history, configuration references and feature flags independently, then identify the exact subset approved for activation. Review source tests for constructor wiring and schema qualification because a service can compile while failing to start against its intended schema. Preserve applied Flyway files. Capture immutable source/image identifiers, previous healthy revision and one-replica settings before any real deployment; Academy publication itself must not update this service.

steps.label: Enterprise failure analysis: reconcile occurrences before replaying workers
steps.detail: When a meal is missing, inspect the customer's subscription, cycle eligibility, schedule, occurrence record, order-command state and callback result in order. When duplicates appear, stop further harm and preserve both internal and external references. Do not delete an occurrence or payment record to make a scheduled worker start over. A code rollback may leave already created orders and payments that still require normal fulfillment or an approved correction. Recovery must distinguish stale projections from actual duplicate commitments. A new replica or a wider scheduling window is not a substitute for identifying the failed invariant.

steps.label: Enterprise lab: rehearse a lifecycle incident
steps.detail: Prepare three synthetic incidents: no paid cycle, an occurrence persisted before a process restart, and an order callback delayed after creation. For each, record the first failing boundary, expected record count, prohibited duplicate action, safe next read and recovery. Run the selected ownership, schedule-validation and paid-cycle tests. Add a release matrix covering dormant flags, migration history, exact source/artifact, backward compatibility and rollback. Leave real database, provider and authenticated production fields unclaimed unless actually tested. The exercise must not trigger a billing run, activate a scheduler or create a customer order.

lessons.lab: Completion evidence: an auditable lifecycle recovery packet with executed/skipped tests and a rollback that preserves financial and fulfillment history. Completing this course does not approve new subscription economics.
